questions.question: What is @InjectMocks in Mockito and how does it work?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Mockito Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: `@InjectMocks` asks Mockito to create or reuse the object under test and inject declared mocks or spies. It first considers the largest constructor. If constructor injection creates the object, Mockito does not continue with setter and field injection; otherwise it may try setters and then fields. It is best-effort convenience, not a full dependency-injection container, so direct constructor wiring is often clearer.

sections.title: How @InjectMocks Automates Test Setup
sections.content:
`@InjectMocks` is a Mockito convenience for constructing or reusing the subject and placing declared mocks or spies into it. It does not behave like Spring's dependency-injection container and does not guarantee that every required collaborator was found.

Mockito first considers the largest constructor and resolves parameters from available mocks by type. If construction succeeds, it stops rather than also running setter and field injection. If constructor injection is not used, Mockito can try property/setter injection and then field injection on a usable instance.

Unmatched collaborators can remain null, while an unusable target type or a constructor that throws can fail setup. For a class with a clear constructor, `new OrderService(repository, gateway)` is often the simplest and most explicit test wiring.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|InjectMocks|~Builds the subject|collects Mock fields|injects automatically|constructor preferred
blue|How It Picks|~Order matters|constructor, setter, field|by type then name|silent on failure
emerald|Gotcha|~Null dependencies|when no match|prefer constructor|or wire by hand

sections.title: InjectMocks with Constructor Injection
When to Use @InjectMocks
sections.content:
Use **@InjectMocks** in every unit test for service classes with multiple dependencies. It eliminates boilerplate setup code and makes tests cleaner. This is standard for testing Spring services annotated with @Service or @Component.

Use constructor injection in your production code (the preferred Spring pattern) and @InjectMocks will match it automatically.

Avoid @InjectMocks when your class has complex initialization logic beyond dependency injection—like builders, factory methods, or constructor parameters that aren't dependencies. In those cases, manually instantiate with new and pass mocks explicitly. Also skip it when writing integration tests with @SpringBootTest, where Spring's real context should handle injection. @InjectMocks is purely for isolated unit tests with Mockito.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: Without this annotation on the test class, Mockito's annotation processing never runs. Your @Mock fields become null, and @InjectMocks doesn't create the object, causing NullPointerException on the first line of your test. Always pair these two annotations.
- **Silent injection failure**: If your class has no matching constructor, no setters, and private final fields, all three injection strategies fail. Mockito creates the object anyway with null dependencies. Your test compiles but crashes at runtime. Enable Mockito's strict mode or write a setup assertion checking dependencies aren't null.
- **Mixing @InjectMocks with manual instantiation**: Writing @InjectMocks private OrderService service = new OrderService(...) defeats the purpose. Remove the = new part and let Mockito handle it entirely.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Purpose**: creates or reuses the subject and injects declared mocks or spies
- **Constructor first**: considers the largest constructor
- **Stops on success**: successful constructor injection is not followed by setter or field injection
- **Fallbacks**: setter/property, then field injection when applicable
- **Best effort**: unmatched dependencies can remain null; direct constructor wiring is clearer for required dependencies

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `@InjectMocks` is a convenience for wiring the class under test from the mocks and spies declared in the test. Mockito first considers the largest constructor and resolves its parameters by type. If it creates the object through that constructor, it does not continue into setter and field injection. If constructor injection is not used, it can try setters and then fields. This is best-effort wiring, not a full dependency-injection container, so an unmatched collaborator can remain null. For a simple service I often prefer `new OrderService(repository, gateway)` because the compiler checks the constructor and the wiring is visible. `@InjectMocks` is useful when that convenience stays unambiguous.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock and @Spy in Mockito?
questions.title: @Mock vs @Spy Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @Mock creates a fully fake object where all methods return default values (null, 0, false) unless stubbed. @Spy wraps a real object instance where unstubbed methods call the real implementation; only configured methods are overridden. Use @Spy when you need partial mocking of a real object.

sections.title: Understanding Mock vs Spy in Mockito
sections.content:
When writing unit tests for Spring services, you need to isolate your class from its dependencies. **@Mock** creates a completely hollow shell—a fake object where every method returns Java's default values (null for objects, 0 for numbers, false for booleans) unless you explicitly tell it what to return.

Think of it like a mannequin in a store: it looks like a person but does nothing on its own. **@Spy**, on the other hand, is a real object wrapped in Mockito's recording layer. It's like having your actual teammate do their job, but you can tap them on the shoulder and say "for this one task, do it my way instead." Unstubbed methods execute the real code. Use @Mock when you don't want any real logic running—just fake responses. Use @Spy when the real implementation is mostly correct but you need to override specific methods like database calls or HTTP requests during testing.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the Mock annotation|~A full fake|all methods stubbed|return defaults|no real code runs
blue|the Spy annotation|~A real object wrapped|real methods run|stub selectively|a partial mock
emerald|Spy Gotcha|~Use do return|when calls the real method|side effects fire|prefer mock if unsure

sections.title: Mock vs Spy Behavior Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | @Mock | @Spy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Object Creation | Fully fake hollow object | Wraps real object instance |
| Unstubbed Method Behavior | Returns null/0/false defaults | Executes real method implementation |
| Stubbing Requirement | Must stub every needed method | Only stub methods you want overridden |
| Use Case | Complete isolation from dependencies | Partial mocking of real objects |
| Performance | Fastest—no real code runs | Slower—real code executes for unstubbed methods |

sections.title: Mock and Spy in Action
Choosing Between Mock and Spy
sections.content:
Use **@Mock** when testing business logic that depends on external systems like databases, REST clients, or message queues—you want zero real interaction. For example, testing OrderService that calls OrderRepository should mock the repository so no database queries run.

Use **@Spy** when working with utility classes or legacy services where most logic is correct but you need to fake specific slow or flaky methods. If you're testing a PaymentService that validates card numbers (fast, no side effects) but also calls a third-party fraud API (slow, unreliable), spy the service and stub only the fraud check method. Another common case: testing a class with private helper methods you want to keep real while faking only the collaborators.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using a spy as the default**: unstubbed real methods may perform I/O, mutate state, or throw.
- **Assuming `@Spy` always needs an initializer**: Mockito can construct a suitable class, but explicit construction is clearer when chosen state or constructor arguments matter.
- **Eager stubbing on a spy**: `when(spy.method())` invokes the real method during setup; use a `do...when` form when that call is unsafe.
- **Saying `doReturn` is always required**: ordinary `when` can work when the real setup call is harmless.
- **Spying the subject to avoid good design**: extracting an external operation into a collaborator often gives a cleaner test.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **@Mock**: creates empty shell object returning default values (null, 0, false) for all methods unless stubbed
- **@Spy**: wraps real object instance where unstubbed methods execute actual implementation code
- **Stubbing requirement**: mocks need explicit stubbing for every call; spies only need stubs for overridden behavior
- **Isolation principle**: prefer @Mock for dependencies to keep tests fast and isolated from external systems
- **Partial mocking**: use @Spy when you need most real behavior but must fake specific expensive operations

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I'd say at-Mock creates a completely fake object where every method returns default values like null or zero unless you stub it. It's like a hollow shell. At-Spy is different—it wraps a real object, so unstubbed methods actually run the real code. You only stub the methods you want to override. Here's when you'd use each. If you're testing an OrderService that talks to a database repository, you'd mock the repository because you don't want real database calls in unit tests. The mock gives you full control—you tell it exactly what to return. But let's say you have a PaymentService with ten methods, nine of them are simple calculations, and only one calls an external fraud detection API. You'd spy the PaymentService so the nine calculation methods run normally, and you'd stub only that one slow API call. The common mistake freshers make is using spy everywhere thinking it's safer because it runs real code. But that defeats the purpose of unit testing. You end up with slow tests that hit real systems. Another gotcha is forgetting to initialize the spy with an actual object—at-Spy needs something real to wrap, like at-Spy private EmailValidator validator equals new EmailValidator. Without that, you get null pointer exceptions. So the rule of thumb: mock your dependencies for isolation, spy only when you need partial mocking of the class under test itself.

questions.question: What is a test double and what are the different types?
questions.title: Test Double Types | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A test double is any object used in place of a collaborator during a test. Common roles are dummy, stub, fake, spy, and mock. The words describe how the double is used: a stub supplies answers, a fake has simplified working behavior, and a mock verifies expected interactions. In Mockito specifically, `spy(realObject)` means a partial mock that calls the real object by default; that is narrower than some classic uses of the word test spy.

sections.title: The Five Types of Test Doubles
sections.content:
A **test double** is an object that stands in for a collaborator. The familiar names describe the role it plays in a test rather than a required framework class.

- A **dummy** is passed only to satisfy a parameter and is not used.
- A **stub** supplies prepared answers.
- A **fake** is a simplified working implementation, such as a `Map`-backed repository.
- A **test spy** records information that a test can inspect later.
- A **mock object** is configured around expected interactions and verifies them.

Mockito combines roles: the same Mockito object can supply stubbed answers and record calls for verification. Mockito also uses `spy(realObject)` for a partial mock whose unstubbed methods call real code. That library-specific meaning should not be confused with every use of “test spy” in general testing vocabulary.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Test Double|~Umbrella term|any fake stand-in|five sub-types|the Meszaros taxonomy
blue|The Types|~Each has a role|dummy, stub, fake|spy and mock|mock verifies
emerald|In Mockito|~mock and spy|mock is a full fake|spy wraps a real object|stub via when

sections.title: Five Test Doubles in Mockito
Choosing the Right Test Double
sections.content:
Use **Dummy** when a constructor or method requires a parameter you won't use in the test—mock it with no stubbing.

Use **Stub** when you need consistent fake data returned from a dependency, like a repository always returning the same Order object. This is 80% of Mockito usage.

Use **Fake** when the real implementation is too slow or complex but you need working logic—for example, an InMemoryUserRepository instead of PostgreSQL for integration tests.

Use **Mock** (with verify) when the test's purpose is confirming an interaction happened, like ensuring EmailService.send was called when an order completes.

Use **Spy** when testing a class where you want real methods to execute except for a few specific ones you need to control, like stubbing a slow API call in an otherwise fast service.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling everything a mock**: Freshers say "I'm mocking the repository" when they're actually stubbing it with when().thenReturn(). A true mock uses verify() to assert interactions. Imprecise language suggests unclear thinking about what the test validates.
- **Overusing verify()**: Writing verify() on every mock turns unit tests into fragile change detectors. Only verify interactions that matter to the test's purpose—if you're testing order totals, verifying that logger.info was called is noise.
- **Not knowing when to use Fakes**: Freshers mock everything when a simple Fake (like an in-memory list) would make tests clearer. If your test setup has ten when() statements recreating a repository's behavior, you need a Fake implementation instead.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Test double**: umbrella term for an object standing in for a collaborator
- **Dummy**: unused placeholder
- **Stub**: prepared answers
- **Fake**: simplified working implementation
- **Spy / mock vocabulary**: roles vary; Mockito's `spy` is specifically a partial mock of a real object

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A test double is any object used instead of a real collaborator during a test. A dummy only fills a parameter. A stub returns prepared data. A fake has a small working implementation, such as a `Map`-backed repository. A test spy records information for later checks, while a mock is used to verify expected interactions. These are roles, so one object can play more than one. A Mockito mock, for example, can both return stubbed values and record calls for `verify`. Mockito also uses the term spy for `spy(realObject)`, a partial mock where unstubbed methods call the real object. I keep that library meaning separate from the broader vocabulary.

questions.question: How do you use doReturn().when() vs when().thenReturn() in Mockito?
questions.title: doReturn vs when thenReturn Mockito | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Both forms can stub a non-void method. `when(spy.read()).thenReturn(value)` evaluates `spy.read()` during setup, so a spy's real method runs first. `doReturn(value).when(spy).read()` installs the stub without that call. Prefer the usual `when(...).thenReturn(...)` for ordinary mocks and for safe spy calls; use `doReturn` when invoking the real spy method during setup would fail or cause side effects. Void methods use `doNothing`, `doThrow`, or `doAnswer`, not `doReturn`.

sections.title: Two Stubbing Syntaxes in Mockito
sections.content:
`when(mock.load()).thenReturn(value)` is Mockito's normal stubbing style for a non-void method. The expression inside `when` is evaluated as Java code during setup.

That evaluation is harmless for a regular mock because the method body does not run. On a spy, however, unstubbed methods call the real object, so `when(spy.get(0))` may run real code before Mockito installs the stub. `doReturn(value).when(spy).get(0)` records the same non-void stub without invoking the real method at setup time.

Use `doReturn` when the eager real call is unsafe or impossible. It is not required for every spy. Void methods use the separate `doNothing`, `doThrow`, and `doAnswer` family.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|when then return|~Readable, type-safe|default on mocks|calls real on spies|risky for spies
blue|do return when|~No real call|safe on spies|stubs void|skips the type check
emerald|The Rule|~Mocks use when|spies use do return|avoid spy side effects|same outcome

sections.title: when().thenReturn() vs doReturn().when()
sections.content:
| Aspect | when().thenReturn() | doReturn().when() |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syntax Style | BDD-style, reads naturally | Arrangement-style, more explicit |
| Method Invocation | Calls real method during stubbing | Never calls real method |
| With @Mock | Safe—method already fake | Safe—method already fake |
| With @Spy | Dangerous—real method executes | Safe—method not executed |
| Exception Handling | Real exceptions thrown during setup | No exceptions during setup |
| Type Safety | Compile-time checked return type | Return type checked at runtime |

sections.title: Syntax Difference with Spies
Choosing the Right Syntax
sections.content: Use **when().thenReturn()** for @Mock objects when you want natural BDD-style readability. It reads like English: "when this method is called, then return this value." Most Mockito examples use this syntax because it's intuitive. But always switch to **doReturn().when()** when working with @Spy objects. The moment you spy on a real object, the risk of unintended execution appears. Even if the real method seems harmless now, future changes might add side effects. As a safe rule: if you see @Spy, use doReturn().when(). Also use doReturn().when() when stubbing void methods or methods that throw exceptions, because the when() syntax doesn't work syntactically for those cases—you need doNothing().when() or doThrow().when() instead, which are the same family as doReturn().

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using when().thenReturn() with spies**: This is the number one mistake. Freshers copy-paste stubbing code from mock examples and apply it to spies. The real method runs during test setup, throws an exception or triggers a database call, and the test fails mysteriously before the actual test logic executes. Always grep for @Spy in your test class and verify you're using doReturn syntax.
- **Not understanding when() evaluates the call**: Freshers think when(spy.method()) is just syntax, not an actual method invocation. It's not magic—Java executes that method call to determine what you're stubbing. For spies, that means real code runs.
- **Inconsistent syntax mixing**: Using when().thenReturn() for some stubs and doReturn().when() for others in the same test without reason creates confusion. Pick doReturn consistently for spies, when consistently for mocks.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `when(...).thenReturn(...)` is the normal non-void stubbing style.
- On a spy, the method expression inside `when` runs the real method during setup.
- `doReturn(...).when(spy)...` avoids that eager call.
- Use `doReturn` only when needed; it has weaker compile-time type checking.
- Void methods use `doNothing`, `doThrow`, or `doAnswer`, not `doReturn`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Both syntaxes stub a non-void method, but they differ during setup. In `when(spy.read()).thenReturn(value)`, Java evaluates `spy.read()` before Mockito completes the stubbing. A normal mock returns a default value, but a spy calls the real method, which may access a database, mutate state, or throw.

`doReturn(value).when(spy).read()` installs the stub without executing `read` during setup. For example, stubbing `spyList.get(0)` on an empty real list needs `doReturn("first").when(spyList).get(0)` to avoid `IndexOutOfBoundsException`.

I use the ordinary `when` style for regular mocks and for spy methods that are safe to call. I use `doReturn` only for the unsafe eager-call case, because it provides less compile-time type checking. Void methods are different: they use `doNothing`, `doThrow`, or `doAnswer`.

questions.question: When would you use a Spy instead of a Mock?
questions.title: When to Use a Spy
questions.direct_answer: Use a spy when you deliberately want a real object's methods to run by default while stubbing or verifying a small, specific part of its behavior. A mock starts with Mockito defaults instead. A spy is useful around legacy code or for observing a real collaborator, but real methods can have side effects. `doReturn(...).when(spy)...` avoids calling a risky real method during setup; ordinary `when(...)` can still be used when that setup call is safe.

sections.title: Spy vs Mock: Partial vs Full Isolation
sections.content:
A Mockito **spy** delegates unstubbed calls to a real object. A **mock** uses Mockito's default answers until behavior is stubbed. A spy therefore keeps real behavior while allowing selected calls to be observed or replaced.

That can help when working with legacy code or when a test needs most behavior of a concrete object. It also carries risk: a real method can write a file, call a network service, change state, or fail during test setup.

The normal `when(spy.method()).thenReturn(value)` form evaluates `spy.method()` while configuring the stub. Use `doReturn(value).when(spy).method()` when that real call would be unsafe. If the call is harmless, the normal form is not forbidden. When extensive partial stubbing is required, extracting a collaborator is often clearer than adding more spy rules.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Use a Spy|~Mostly real behaviour|stub one method|legacy code|a partial mock
blue|Use a Mock|~Full isolation|no real code|the simplest default|most unit tests
emerald|Spy Caution|~Real methods run|use do return to stub|watch side effects|a smell if heavy

sections.title: Spy vs Mock in Action
Step 1: Does Your Test Need Real Business Logic?
sections.content: Ask yourself: do I need the actual implementation to run? If you're testing **OrderService** and it depends on **EmailService**, you probably don't want real emails sent—use a **Mock**. But if you're testing **CompositeValidator** that chains multiple validation rules, and you only want to fake one external API call inside one validator, use a **Spy** on the whole validator and stub just that problematic method. Rule of thumb: if you need zero real behavior from a dependency, Mock it. If you need most methods to work normally but want to intercept a few, Spy it. Spies are common in integration tests where you want to keep most of the application stack running but replace a single external call like a third-party HTTP client.

sections.title: Step 2: Can You Refactor Instead of Using Spy?
sections.content: Before reaching for a Spy, consider if your design could be improved. If you're spying on a class because you can't cleanly mock its dependencies, that's a **code smell**—the class might be doing too much or have hard-coded dependencies. Extract the problematic behavior into an interface you can mock. Spies are often a pragmatic choice for **legacy code** where refactoring is too risky or time-consuming, but for new code, they usually signal that you haven't properly separated concerns. If you find yourself stubbing more than 1-2 methods on a Spy, you probably should be using a full Mock or refactoring the class. Spies are a tool for specific situations, not a default choice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting real behavior**: every unstubbed spy method can execute production logic and side effects.
- **Eager setup call**: `when(spy.read()).thenReturn(value)` calls `read()` while configuring the stub; use `doReturn` when that is unsafe.
- **Treating `doReturn` as mandatory**: it is an escape hatch for risky setup calls, not a rule for every spy.
- **Assuming `@Spy` always needs an initializer**: Mockito can construct a suitable type, but explicit construction is clearer when the object needs chosen state or constructor arguments.
- **Hiding a design problem**: heavy partial stubbing may mean a responsibility should be moved behind an injectable collaborator.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Spy**: unstubbed methods call the real implementation
- **Mock**: unstubbed methods use Mockito defaults
- **`doReturn`**: installs a value without invoking the spy's real method during setup
- **Side effects**: inspect real methods before allowing them to run in a unit test
- **Design signal**: many partial stubs can point to a collaborator that should be extracted

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I use a spy when I intentionally need most methods of a real object to run, but I want to replace or verify one small part. A mock is different because unstubbed methods return Mockito defaults. For example, a legacy formatter may have useful real parsing logic but one overridable lookup that reaches a slow external source; a spy can keep the parser and stub that lookup. I first check that the remaining real methods have no unsafe side effects. I also choose the stubbing form carefully: `when(spy.read()).thenReturn(value)` calls the real `read()` during setup, while `doReturn(value).when(spy).read()` does not. `doReturn` is needed only when that setup call is unsafe. If a test needs many partial stubs, I would usually extract the external behavior into a separate dependency and mock that dependency instead.

questions.question: What is a Fake object and how does it differ from a Mock?
questions.title: Fake Object vs Mock
questions.direct_answer: A fake is a small working implementation used in tests, such as a `Map`-backed repository that really stores and retrieves values. A Mockito mock is configured per test with stubs and can record interactions for verification. A fake is useful when state should behave consistently across several calls; a mock is useful when a test needs controlled replies or must check a boundary interaction.

sections.title: Fakes Have Real Logic, Mocks Have Expectations
sections.content:
A **fake** is a working but simplified implementation of a dependency's contract. A `Map`-backed `UserRepository`, for example, can really save a user and return it from a later lookup. The test observes state and returned results without a database.

A **mock** is normally configured for the current test. Mockito can return a chosen value and record calls so the test can verify an interaction such as `mailSender.send(message)`. It does not automatically reproduce the real collaborator's stateful rules.

An embedded database such as H2 is a real database product used as a substitute. It can be useful, but calling it a fake repository hides an important boundary: its SQL dialect and behavior may differ from the production database. Use an application-level fake when its deliberately small contract is enough, and an integration test against the real database technology when database behavior is what must be proved.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Fake|~A light implementation|an in-memory map|real logic, simplified|stateful
blue|Mock|~A programmed fake|returns set values|verifies calls|no real logic
emerald|Pick Rule|~Fake for stateful deps|an in-memory repo|mock for boundaries|external systems

sections.title: Fake Repository vs Mocked Repository
When to Choose Fake vs Mock
sections.content:
Use a **fake** when several operations need consistent state. A small in-memory repository makes workflows such as save → find → reject duplicate easy to exercise without scripting every call.

Use a **mock** when the collaborator is a boundary and the result or interaction is narrow. A mail gateway can return a chosen response, and the test can verify that the expected message was sent once.

A fake needs its own tests because it can drift from the production implementation. It should implement only the contract needed by tests, not attempt to reproduce an entire database or external system.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling an alternative database a perfect fake**: H2 is a real database with its own dialect; passing tests do not prove PostgreSQL or MySQL behavior.
- **Copying production complexity**: a fake should stay small and focused on the relevant contract.
- **Letting a fake drift**: run shared contract tests against the fake and real implementation where practical.
- **Over-scripting a mock**: a long sequence of stateful stubs may be clearer as a small fake.
- **Verifying every call**: verify only interactions that are observable requirements.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Fake**: a simplified implementation with working behavior and state
- **Mock**: configured responses plus optional interaction verification
- **Fake example**: a `Map`-backed repository that really saves and finds values
- **Mock example**: a mail gateway stubbed to respond and verified once
- **Boundary**: a different embedded database is not proof of production-database compatibility

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A fake is a small working implementation of a dependency. For example, a `Map`-backed repository can assign an ID, store a user, and return it from a later lookup. A Mockito mock is configured for a test with calls such as `when(...).thenReturn(...)`, and it can record interactions for `verify(...)`. I prefer a fake when a workflow needs consistent state across several calls, such as saving and then checking for a duplicate. I prefer a mock when I need one controlled response or want to prove an observable boundary interaction, such as sending one email. The trade-off is that a fake can drift from the production implementation, so shared contract tests are useful. I would not treat H2 as proof that production PostgreSQL behavior is correct; H2 is a separate real database with its own behavior.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpyBean and @MockBean in a Spring Boot test?
questions.title: @SpyBean vs @MockBean in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The older Spring Boot `@MockBean` replaces a bean in the test `ApplicationContext` with a Mockito mock; `@SpyBean` wraps an existing bean with a spy so unstubbed calls use real behavior. Since Spring Boot 3.4 these annotations are deprecated for removal in 4.0 in favor of Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean`. A bean override changes the context cache key, but it does not automatically mark every context dirty or force a reload for every test class; classes with the same configuration can reuse a cached context.

sections.title: Spring Context Integration: Full Replacement vs Partial Wrapping
sections.content:
A context-level **mock bean** replaces a matching Spring bean with a Mockito mock. A context-level **spy bean** wraps a real bean so unstubbed methods continue to run real code while selected methods can be stubbed or verified.

Spring Boot's `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean` were deprecated in 3.4 for removal in 4.0. Current Spring Framework provides `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` for the same main roles.

These overrides become part of the Spring test context configuration. Different override sets can create different cache keys and therefore more contexts, but an override does not itself mark the context dirty. Test classes with equivalent configuration can reuse the cached context. Use a plain `@Mock` whenever Spring wiring is not part of the test.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|MockitoBean|~Full mock in context|replaces a bean|unstubbed defaults|current Spring API
blue|MockitoSpyBean|~Wraps a real bean|real methods run|stub selectively|watch side effects
emerald|Context Effect|~Overrides shape configuration|cache key can differ|not automatically dirty|plain Mockito when possible

sections.title: Code Example
MockBean vs SpyBean Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | `@MockitoBean` | `@MockitoSpyBean` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Context role | Overrides with a mock | Overrides by wrapping a real bean with a spy |
| Unstubbed call | Mockito default answer | Real implementation runs |
| Main use | complete controlled replacement | observe or replace selected real behavior |
| Cache effect | override metadata contributes to context key | override metadata contributes to context key |
| Legacy Boot name | `@MockBean` | `@SpyBean` |

sections.title: When to Choose Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **`@MockitoBean`** when a Spring slice or context test needs a controlled replacement for a collaborator. Use **`@MockitoSpyBean`** only when the real bean must continue to run and the test needs to observe or replace selected behavior.

A spy can execute database, HTTP, or other side effects through unstubbed methods, so inspect the real bean carefully. If the test only exercises one service with replaceable dependencies, a plain Mockito test is usually a clearer boundary and needs no Spring context.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using context overrides for plain unit tests**: direct constructor wiring is enough when Spring behavior is irrelevant.
- **Spying an unsafe bean**: unstubbed methods can perform real external work.
- **Using normal `when` on a risky spy call**: it executes the real method during setup; use a `do...when` form when needed.
- **Calling every cache difference invalidation**: override metadata can create a different cache key, but does not automatically mark a context dirty.
- **Using legacy annotations in new code**: current Spring uses `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean`.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A context mock replaces a Spring bean; a context spy wraps real behavior.
- `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean` are deprecated since Boot 3.4 for removal in 4.0.
- Prefer `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` in current Spring tests.
- Bean overrides affect the test context cache key; they do not automatically call `@DirtiesContext`.
- Spy stubbing may execute real code unless the `do...when` style is used.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Spring context mock replaces a bean with a Mockito mock, so unstubbed methods return Mockito defaults. A context spy wraps the existing bean, so unstubbed methods run the real implementation and only selected behavior is overridden or verified.

The older Spring Boot annotations are `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean`. They were deprecated in Spring Boot 3.4 for removal in 4.0 in favor of Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean`. The choice still depends on whether the test wants a complete replacement or mostly real behavior.

Bean overrides form part of the test context configuration. Different override combinations can produce different cache keys and slow a suite by creating more contexts, but they do not automatically dirty every context. Equivalent test configurations can reuse a cached context. With a spy, I use the `doReturn` or `doThrow` style when normal `when` would execute the real bean during setup.

questions.question: Can you spy on a final class or a static method in Mockito, and how?
questions.title: Mocking Final Classes and Static Methods
questions.direct_answer: Modern Mockito can mock or spy final classes and final instance methods when the inline mock maker is active; Mockito 5 uses inline mocking by default. Static methods are not spied on as part of an object. Use `Mockito.mockStatic(Type.class)` to create a scoped `MockedStatic`, configure calls inside a try-with-resources block, and close it so the thread-local static behavior does not leak. Some methods and JVM types remain unsupported, and frequent static mocking can signal a hard-to-test design.

sections.title: Extended Mocking Capabilities with Trade-offs
sections.content:
Mockito's inline mock maker can instrument final classes and final instance methods. In Mockito 5 it is the default mock maker, so a separate `mockito-inline` artifact is normally unnecessary.

A static method belongs to a class rather than an object, so it is not “spied” through `@Spy`. `Mockito.mockStatic(ClockProvider.class)` returns a `MockedStatic<ClockProvider>`. Stubbing and verification apply only within that scope and on the creating thread. Use try-with-resources so the scope always closes.

Inline instrumentation has limits: native methods cannot be mocked, some core JVM types are restricted, and interactions with agents or unusual runtimes may need configuration. A small scoped static mock can help around legacy code, but an injected clock or gateway is usually easier to test.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Final Types|~Supported by inline mock maker|default in Mockito 5|ordinary mock or spy|older setups may differ
blue|Static Calls|~Use mockStatic|scoped MockedStatic|close after test|thread-local scope
emerald|Design Boundary|~Prefer an injectable collaborator|avoid global state|use static mocking narrowly|verify behavior

sections.title: Mocking Final Classes and Static Methods
When These Features Are Justified
sections.content:
Modern Mockito can mock final types when the inline mock maker is active; Mockito 5 uses it by default. Older Mockito versions or custom mock-maker configurations may need different setup.

Use `mockStatic` for a narrow legacy seam that cannot yet be injected. Keep the `MockedStatic` inside try-with-resources so it is closed promptly. If many tests replace the same static call, introduce a small collaborator such as `AppClock` or `IdGenerator` and test through that interface instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding `mockito-inline` automatically**: Mockito 5 uses the inline mock maker by default; check the actual version and configuration first.
- **Leaking a static mock**: always close `MockedStatic`, normally with try-with-resources.
- **Calling static mocking a spy**: `mockStatic` creates a scoped static mock, not an object spy.
- **Using static mocking everywhere**: repeated global seams are usually clearer behind an injected collaborator.
- **Ignoring limitations**: native methods and some JVM-sensitive targets are not ordinary mock seams.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Mockito 5 uses the inline mock maker by default, enabling final class and final method mocking.
- Static methods use a scoped `MockedStatic`, not an object spy.
- Close static mocks with try-with-resources to prevent leakage.
- Native methods and some core/JVM cases remain unsupported or restricted.
- Prefer injectable collaborators when the static dependency is under part of the design.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Modern Mockito can mock final classes and final instance methods through the inline mock maker, which is the default in Mockito 5. Older projects may need different setup, so the project version and active mock maker matter.

Static methods are handled separately. `Mockito.mockStatic(Type.class)` creates a `MockedStatic` scope. Inside a try-with-resources block I can stub and verify calls; closing the scope restores normal behavior. This is not a spy on an object, and leaving the scope open can leak behavior into later tests on the same thread.

There are limits: native methods cannot be mocked and some JVM/core types are restricted. Static mocking is useful for a narrow legacy seam, but if many tests need it, an injected clock, ID generator, or gateway usually gives clearer design and simpler tests.
